As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. This paper does not advocate technological restraint, but seeks to clarify the structural conditions under which accountability protocols become necessary.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. It looks at how accountability is shared among system designers, vendors, deployers, and human operators when AI-driven tools are used to influence detection actions, prioritization, and response. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. WAKE✳︎ GOVERNANCE
================

This module is the mechanical rulebook for WAKE✳︎.

The model is allowed to PROPOSE changes to durable state.
It is never allowed to decide whether those changes are valid.

That distinction is central to the experiment:

    model output = proposal
    governance = authority
    durable state = accepted history

The functions in this file are deliberately deterministic. Given the same
state and the same proposal, governance should reach the same decision
regardless of which model produced the proposal.

A model cannot persuade this module, reinterpret its instructions, waive a
requirement, or edit the rules during an invocation.

A research transition is atomic: an invalid research action rejects that
transition without partial writes. application_policy.py owns the separate
editorial wrapper, which can withhold an invalid final blog while committing
independently valid research. Do not move that exception into the reducer.

This gives WAKE✳︎ an important property:

    failure can become durable information
    without failure becoming durable state.
